They attain hundreds of thousands of samādhis, even up to hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of samādhis.
From this point downward, it clarifies that by virtue of hearing the teaching, they further obtain the *nayuta* concentrations from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage and above.
Having attained samādhi, one travels through various buddha-fields to make offerings to the Buddhas.
Once this samādhi is obtained, one is able to travel through buddha-fields, make offerings to the Buddhas, and hear and receive teachings not previously heard.
They are born in the palaces of the various devas, proclaiming the Triple Gem and manifesting the body of a Buddha.

This makes it clear that these bodhisattvas not only travel through successive lives to make offerings and receive instruction, but are further born in celestial palaces to praise the Triple Gem and manifest the body of a Buddha.
Surrounded by a great assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas,
the Buddha-body manifested through clarity is likewise surrounded by a multitude;
by means of the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind, he delivers sentient beings.

This clarifies what the Buddha has taught: by awakening to the manifestation of one's own mind, one delivers all sentient beings and analytically explains that external natures lack inherent existence;
furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, it is taught that external things have no inherent nature.
He causes them all to remain far removed from views such as existence and non-existence,
in order to transform those to be taught so that they may leave behind the views of the two extremes.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The world is the measure of the mind; when the sons of the Buddha observe it, they see that there is only the measure of the mind.
This is called the "world. I exhort all sons of the Buddha to observe this well.
The body of various manifestations, free from conditioned activity,
responds like a mani jewel, arising without thought;
having attained the powers and superknowledges, it is accomplished with sovereign mastery.
This clarifies the manifestation of transformation bodies, which arises through the attainment of mastery over the powers and supernormal knowledges (*ṛddhivibhūti*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us all dharmas as being empty, unarisen, non-dual, and devoid of the characteristics of intrinsic nature."
Regarding the subsequent section that cites emptiness, non-arising, and so forth: this is intended to reveal the ultimate destination reached through the four preceding gates.

It serves as a formal statement of the core tenet in response to the earlier inquiry, "What is emptiness? By what cause [is it so]? The emptiness now discussed clarifies that the five preceding dharmas do not exist;

being devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their very essence—the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)—is empty. Being non-dual means that both types of self (*ātman*) have perished. Non-arising is intended to clarify the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
They do not arise.
Having awakened to this emptiness— unborn, non-dual, and devoid of the characteristics of intrinsic nature—
we and the other assemblies of bodhisattvas have abandoned the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence.
From here below, the benefits are set forth. This clarifies the departure from delusion;
it quickly attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* clarifies the attainment of the fruit.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
I shall now explain it to you in detail."

The following clarifies that when the Buddha is about to provide an answer, he must first prepare the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) before responding. "Listen attentively" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
"reflect well" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and "keep it in mind" refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.
This explains that since Mahāmati had received the Buddha’s permission and admonition, he responded with reverence and self-discipline.
The word *wei* (唯)—pronounced with the initial *yì* and the vowel *shuǐ*—is a term of respectful response, signifying a humble assent.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Regarding 'emptiness of emptiness' (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), it will be explained extensively below.
This constitutes the general response. That is to say, the initial citation of the gate of emptiness was intended to refer to the remaining three [gates].
Now, by citing 'emptiness' once again, the former 'emptiness' refers back to the preceding question, while the latter 'emptiness' serves as the term of citation."
This refers to the locus of the self-nature of false conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
This explains the essential nature of emptiness: it simply means that the very place where there is false conceptualization of existence is itself emptiness;
there is no other principle involved. The same applies to all other categories.
“Mahāmati, for those who are attached to the imagined nature, I teach emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the absence of self-nature.

This next section clarifies the intent behind these four gates, beginning with emptiness. It is precisely because there is attachment to the imagined existence [of phenomena] that emptiness is taught.”
The remaining three [categories] are to be understood by analogy with this.

Mahāmati, those seven kinds of emptiness have been briefly explained above as a general response to the two questions. Below, the four gates beginning with emptiness will be explained individually; now, first, the gate of emptiness is explained. This...
This is the initial heading. Now, while various sutras explain emptiness with varying degrees of detail, the meaning remains no different even though this present sutra is concise. These are:

the emptiness of marks (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-conditioned activity (*asaṃskāra-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression (*sarvadharma-nirabhilāpya-śūnyatā*). First...
The first is the noble wisdom of the great emptiness of single meaning (*ekārtha-āryajñāna-mahāśūnyatā*).
Next, the seven names are listed.
What is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇaśūnyatā*)?
The third section consists of the citation and explanation. First, it raises the question regarding the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*):
"All natures are empty of their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common-characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
This is the detailed explanation. That is to say, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty of their own-characteristics and common-characteristics; this is the brief statement of the explanation.
By observing how things are accumulated through successive stages, one discerns that they lack intrinsic nature and that their specific and general characteristics do not arise.

Indeed, the phenomena of dependent origination are formed through provisional accumulation; since they are understood to be devoid of intrinsic nature, both specific and general characteristics are non-existent.
Since both self and other lack intrinsic nature, their characteristics do not abide.

As for what are called "characteristics," they all arise from the conjunction of the three. Now, having realized that both self and other likewise lack intrinsic nature, upon what could characteristics depend to abide?
Therefore, it is said that all natures and characteristics are empty.
This concludes the third synthesis.
This is called the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
This is the fourth section.
What is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)?
This is the initial inquiry intended to clarify the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
This refers to the nature of the self.

Since its own-nature (*svabhāva*) is unarisen, when one observes the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) from above, it is found not to exist; now, when observing the specific nature (*viśeṣasvabhāva*), it is likewise non-existent. Therefore, it is said that the nature of the self is unarisen.
This is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
This too is appropriate.
Therefore, it is said that there is the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
The summary can be understood thus.
What is the emptiness of formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*)?
There are three explanations of the emptiness of formations; this is also the first inquiry.
This means that the aggregates (skandhas) are devoid of self and what belongs to a self.
To explain further: "formations" (saṃskāra) refers to the five aggregates. Since the aggregates and formations are empty, "what belongs to a self" does not exist.
[The self] arises through the conditions of causes, effects, actions, and skillful means.

Previously we traced back to the fruit of the aggregates; now we exhaustively investigate their cause. To speak of the fruit of the aggregates, it must be summoned and induced by ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and karma.
Since ignorance has no essential nature (*svabhāva*), upon what could karma and its fruit arise? When both cause and fruit are absent, then the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are non-existent.
This is called the emptiness of activity (*kriyā-śūnyatā*).
This is the summary indication.
Mahāmati, this very emptiness of activity, through its successive dependent origination, is devoid of intrinsic nature; this is called the absence of activity (*akriyā*).
Emptiness.
Next, it clarifies that non-action is also empty. In contrast to the cycle of birth and death characterized by action, nirvana is described as being without action.
Since action itself is ultimately non-existent, how could there be a "non-action" to persist?
What is the emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression?
This now clarifies the fifth [point]. This is the initial inquiry:
because the nature of conceptual construction is ineffable, all phenomena are beyond verbal expression.

This is the next section of the commentary. It clarifies that false conceptualization is the root of language; language arises from false conceptualization. Since one has realized that the nature of false conceptualization is empty, verbal expression is not ultimately existent.
Therefore, all phenomena are beyond words.
This is called the emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression;
this concludes the threefold demonstration.
What is the great emptiness of the ultimate reality of noble wisdom regarding all phenomena?
Sixth, the elucidation of the emptiness of meaning (*artha-śūnyatā*). This also first poses the inquiry:
"That is to say, having attained the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), all views and the latencies (*vāsanā*) of those views are empty.

Next follows the explanation: "That is to say, having attained the wisdom of self-awakening, one understands [reality] as if it were before one's eyes; since present latencies have already perished, [they are thus empty]."
There is nothing that is not quiescent. Thus one knows that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are themselves the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This is called the Great Emptiness of the Noble Wisdom of the Ultimate Truth of All Phenomena.
It is revealed by the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
What is mutual emptiness (*itaretara-śūnyatā*)?

From here below, the seventh [emptiness] is explained. This is the first inquiry. It means that when two phenomena are viewed in relation to one another, each serves as the "other" (*itar*) for the other;
hence it is called "mutual" (*itaretara*).
This means that when something is absent in a certain place, that place is empty of that thing; this is called "emptiness of this and that" (itaretara-śūnyatā).

Next, it is explained by way of phenomena: when a certain object is absent from a particular location, or when a particular location is absent from a certain object, each lacks one side, and thus mutual attachment gives rise to views.
Mahāmati, it is like the house of Mṛgāramātṛ, which has no elephants, horses, oxen, or sheep; yet it is not that there is no community of bhikṣus.
Thus one speaks of its emptiness.
To explain this further through a metaphor: "Mṛgāra" is a personal name, while his mother was the female lay disciple (upāsikā) Viśākhā, who was profoundly devoted [to the Dharma].
Regarding the Three Jewels: one constructs a vihāra and establishes bhikṣus within it. It is called "empty" based on the absence therein of elephants, horses, and other livestock;
it does not mean that the dwelling is empty of the nature of a dwelling, nor that the bhikṣus are empty of the nature of bhikṣus.

This is explained by way of contrast: it is not that there are no monasteries or monks that they are said to be empty; rather, it is simply because there are no elephants or horses that they are said to be empty.
It is not that there are no elephants or horses in other places.
This clarifies that other families possess only elephants and horses but lack bhikṣus; therefore, they are said to be "empty.
This is called the mutual exclusion of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
Below this, the combination of phenomena clarifies how all dharmas mutually exclude one another.
In that [place], there is no that; this is called "emptiness of this and that" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*).
Because they are mutually non-existent, they are termed "this and that.
These are the seven kinds of emptiness.
To summarize the meanings of the seven kinds of emptiness mentioned above:
among them, the "emptiness of this and that" (itaretara-śūnyatā) is the coarsest form of emptiness; you should distance yourself from it.
Desiring to restate this meaning once more, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I have always taught the Dharma of emptiness, which is far removed from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

These two lines of the following two verses summarize the first of the four gates mentioned above; they praise the initial gate of emptiness, clarifying that the meaning of ultimate emptiness taught by the Buddha is by nature free from annihilationism and eternalism.
"Birth and death are like illusions and dreams, yet those karmas do not perish.
These two lines of verse pertain to the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*). They clarify that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are like illusions and are fundamentally unreal.

Furthermore, the statement "those karmas do not perish" intends to clarify that their nature is inherently unestablished. Taken together, these summarize suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) to elucidate non-arising.
"Space and nirvāṇa— The cessation of these two is also like this.

These two lines of verse concern the gate of non-duality. By citing the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena held by the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists, it clarifies that all dualistic extremes are likewise [non-existent].
"Fools engage in false conceptualization; the noble ones are free from existence and non-existence.

These two lines constitute the section on being free from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This means that while fools falsely conceptualize and cling to things as having an intrinsic nature, the noble ones have transcended such notions of existence and non-existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:

"Mahāmati, emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the departure from the marks of self-nature—these universally enter into all the sūtras of the Buddhas. In every sūtra whatsoever, this meaning is fully expounded."
From here below, the four meanings beginning with emptiness are clarified. They penetrate all sūtras; there is not a single dharma that does not contain this principle.
All sūtras, in accordance with the aspirational minds of sentient beings, provide detailed explanations to reveal their meaning.
Yet true reality does not reside in verbal expression.

From this point downward, the provisional is reconciled with and returns to the real. As for those various sutras that do not teach the gateways of emptiness and so forth, it is simply because the aspirations of beings are not uniform and their inclinations differ;
thus, the Buddha responds to their capacities, resulting in these distinctions among the teaching gates. However, the ultimate truth remains...
It lies in mental awakening, not in words and phrases.
It is like the mirage that deceives and deludes a herd of deer; the deer, regarding those signs, cling to the notion of water, yet there is no water there.
This is an illustration. Just as those herds of deer, deceived by the perception of thirst, falsely see a mirage and call it water, though in reality it is not water;
so too all sentient beings, deluded by their false minds, grasp at words and letters as being real.
None are able to turn back from this.
Thus, all the dharmas taught in the sūtras are for the purpose of inspiring joy in the foolish;
they do not represent the true noble wisdom that resides in verbal expression.
This clarifies the correspondence with the Dharma. However, that which is expounded through words and phrases is intended to inspire joy in the ignorant;
true noble wisdom, by contrast, utterly transcends names and expressions.
Therefore, one should rely upon the meaning and not be attached to verbal expressions;
one should be encouraged to rely on the true meaning and not be attached to the literal words.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has spoken in the sūtras..."
The *tathāgatagarbha* is by nature pure and clear; it manifests the thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings.

Regarding the subsequent detailed exposition of the *tathāgatagarbha*, there are several intended meanings: first, to distinguish it from non-Buddhists; second, to harmonize the provisional and the ultimate.
The teaching of the Threefold Knowledge (trividyā) does not contradict emptiness.

In this first question, the ancient teaching is cited, namely that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is inherently pure, endowed with the marks and signs of a Buddha, and fully present within sentient beings; speaking of the fruit in terms of the cause, it is called "transformation and entry."
It is like a precious jewel of great value wrapped in soiled clothing.
First is the Dharma; next is the analogy: just as a precious gold treasure wrapped in filthy raiment is discarded by all who see it, with none able to honor it.
The Tathāgatagarbha is likewise eternally abiding and unchanging;
yet it is enveloped by the aggregates,
elements, and sense bases, which are like a great jewel wrapped in tattered rags, defiled by the dust and toil of unreal conceptualization, greed, hatred, and delusion.

Although the preceding verse and the prose commentary differ in their phrasing, their general intent is to refute the dualistic views of the ultimate and the conventional, thereby leading sentient beings [to realization].
They meet upon the Middle Way.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled in words and meanings."
Now, to clarify the meaning of words: it is intended that one rely on the meaning and not on the words. This is the initial question of Mahāmati, who cites a former teaching:
"What constitutes a bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding words and meanings?"
Next, the skillful means for requesting the meaning of the words is presented.
What are the words? What is the meaning?
These three inquiries concern the characteristics of words and their meanings.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon it well. I shall explain it for you.
In this response of the Buddha, this first section serves as a formal invitation to speak.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.
Then, with reverence, he accepted what was enjoined.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, “What is meant by ‘speech’?”
The *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa* provides a detailed answer. First, regarding the explanation of "speech" (*vāk*):
this clarifies the initial inquiry, namely that speech is a combination of words (*akṣara*) and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Now, explaining "speech" further: it means that the three factors—words, syllables (*akṣara*), and conceptual construction—are combined to constitute the characteristic of speech.
Depending on the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, gums, and cheeks, and subsequently depending on these eight factors such as the throat, speech is produced; this clarifies the conditions for language.
It arises from the habitual tendencies of the false conceptualizations of "I" and "mine" involved in such speech.
Third, the mutual relation between self and other, as well as long-standing verbal habits—these together are the causes for the utterance of speech;
this is what is called "speech.
Third, the summary indication.
Mahāmati, what is meant by "meaning" (*artha*)?

This is the third explanation of meaning; it is also the initial inquiry, which refers to being free from all characteristics of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and characteristics of verbal expression (*abhilāpa*).
Next is the formal explanation of the meaning. The phrase "free from delusion and speech" clarifies that the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity has ceased;
this is the inconceivable, supreme meaning.
This is what is called "meaning.
To conclude by way of summary:
Mahāmati, regarding such meaning, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in a solitary and quiet place, relies upon the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Self-awakened and aware, one heads toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
This clarifies the meaning of the skillful means of cultivation.

Once the body of habitual tendencies has been transformed, one self-awakens to the state of the object of perception and contemplates the characteristics of the progressive advancement through each stage and the intervals between them.
This means that by cultivating the meaning, one obtains benefit;
this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skill in meaning.
Third, the summary conclusion.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who is skilled in words and meaning contemplates that words and meaning are neither different nor not different;
he contemplates meaning and words in the same manner.
Now, to clarify the characteristics of the relationship between words and their meanings: this is the general initial heading.
If the word were different from the meaning, this would now cite the divergent views.
Thus, meaning is not distinguished by means of words;

for if things were different, they would be fundamentally disparate. How could meaning be distinguished by means of words? This is a refutation showing that the distinction between meanings cannot be established, yet you attempt to enter into meaning by means of words.
We observe in the world that one enters into meaning by means of words; since word and meaning are mutually dependent, they cannot be said to be different.
This is a consistent explanation, just as a lamp illuminates forms.
However, as for entering into the meaning through the words, it is like seeing forms by means of a lamp; one cannot say they are different.
If one refutes their non-difference, the logic follows exactly as before, differing only in its direction. Is not the subtlety of the Sanskrit text found precisely here?
Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding the non-arising and non-ceasing intrinsic nature of nirvāṇa, the three vehicles, the one vehicle, the mind, and the self-nature:
the present mention of the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing, as well as the three vehicles, the one vehicle, and the equality of the nature of the mind, has two intended meanings.

First, it clarifies that the meaning of the preceding statements is no different [from the present]. Second, it serves to briefly eliminate the fault of dualistic views; this meaning encompasses what was stated above.
Below. As with the attachment to the meaning of conventional expressions, one falls into the extremes of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*).

This clarifies two views; that is to say, as worldly ordinary persons do, by relying on words they conceptualize meanings, and thus inevitably fall into the two extremes of superimposition and denial.

If one reckons that the referent of words exists, one establishes what is to be subsumed; yet if one further claims that both word and referent are non-existent, this is likewise equivalent to repudiation.
This is a brief indication of the point.
"Seeing difference and establishing difference through false discrimination" is the explanation.
If one perceives that words and meanings are different, one establishes them as being different;
this is one form of false discrimination, and other cases may be understood by analogy with this.
"Various delusive thoughts appear like a magical illusion.

From this point on, he provides an illustration; this is a brief indication. For example, regarding the methods of magic and the person created by magic, whether one speaks of their identity or difference, these are merely manifestations of the delusive thoughts of the ignorant.
For example, various illusions cause ordinary, foolish beings to form divergent false conceptions; this is not the case for the noble ones.
This is a broad analogy. If one perceives the illusion and the illusory object as being either identical or distinct, such is the knowledge of the ordinary fool, not that of the noble sages.
The same applies to the conceptualization of words and their meanings. However, for the noble ones, from the very beginning...
Since they do not abide in words or meanings, how could there be any identity or difference? Are they not the same as an illusion?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Those who, through the conceptualization of verbal expression, establish various phenomena—because of that establishment, they fall into the hells after death.
This clarifies death.
The foolish and deluded conceive of phenomena based on their own sentiments; karmic retribution arises accordingly. The same applies to slander. The text is abbreviated and not fully set forth.
[End of section]. *Niraya*. In the original Sanskrit, it is called *naraka*, meaning "that which is oppressed by manifold sufferings"; here it is translated as "hell.
Within the aggregates (*skandha*), there is no self; the aggregates are not themselves the self; yet it is not as those deluded thoughts imagine, nor is it that there is no self at all.

Because the proponents of the "Person" (pudgala) maintain that the meaning of the term [refers to] identity or difference, one borrows their own theory of the self within the aggregates (skandhas) as an analogy to refute them.

"All things possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), just like the deluded imaginings of the foolish"—this clarifies the concessive argument (*anujñā*). If the referents of all words possessed an intrinsic nature, just like the aggregates and the self imagined by the foolish, then...
If it were as they perceive it, then everyone should perceive the Truth;

this [argument] refutes [the opponent's view] by comparing it to others. That is to say, if one calculates that the referent of words (*śabdārtha*) is like the aggregates (*skandha*) and the self (*ātman*), then all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) should perceive the Truth.
However, since non-Buddhists do not perceive the Truth, we know that those who cling to the referent of words likewise [do not perceive it].
Thus it is:
all phenomena are without intrinsic nature; purity and impurity are entirely non-existent. They are unreal as they are perceived, yet they are not nothingness.
This is a general exegesis in accordance with the text: the first two lines indicate existence, while the final line negates non-existence; together they clarify the Middle Way.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The following section extensively clarifies "knowledge" (*vijñāna*) in order to ensure reliance on wisdom (*jñāna*) rather than on consciousness.
It provides the initial enumeration in response to the preceding question regarding how many kinds of wisdom there are.
If one skillfully discriminates the characteristics of knowledge and consciousness,
then you and all bodhisattvas will be able to penetrate the characteristics of knowledge and consciousness, as you yourselves have asserted.
Raising up the benefit of the universal Dharma:
swiftly attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This clarifies the benefit of obtaining the fruit.
Mahāmati, that wisdom is of three kinds.
In the detailed explanation of its characteristics, this first section indicates their number:
namely, mundane, supramundane, and the highest supramundane.
Next, their number is enumerated.
What is mundane knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*)?
This is the inquiry that introduces the explanation of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*). First, there is this inquiry regarding mundane knowledge.
This refers to all non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings who cling to the views of existence and non-existence.
To explain further: those who, out of ignorance, merely speculate on existence and non-existence possess only mundane wisdom.
What, then, is supramundane wisdom?
Next, the supramundane is explained. This is also preceded by an inquiry:
namely, that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into attachment to their own and common characteristics, harboring hopes and fixations.
Furthermore, those of the two vehicles reckon the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as being existent.
What is supramundane, most excellent wisdom?
To clarify what is most excellent, this is also the initial inquiry.

It refers to how all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas contemplate the dharma of non-existence, perceive that which is neither arising nor ceasing, and remain free from the categories of existence and non-existence.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas clearly illuminate reality as it is; they perceive all phenomena as fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing, and as abiding neither in existence nor non-existence.
This is the supreme wisdom. Generally speaking, the three types [of wisdom] are elucidated in order to manifest their excellence and encourage their cultivation.
Entering the stage of the Tathāgata, wherein the non-self of persons and phenomena arises through self-realization,
and attaining the realization of the two emptinesses at the stage of Buddhahood— this is accomplished through the diligent cultivation of self-awakening.
Mahāmati, that which arises and ceases is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which does not arise and does not cease is wisdom (*jñāna*).
This has clarified the distinction between the superior and the wise. Now, I shall distinguish the relative excellence of wisdom and consciousness; this first pair may be understood thus.

Falling into the marks of the signless, as well as falling into the various marks of existence and non-existence, is consciousness (*vijñāna*); transcending the marks of existence and non-existence is wisdom (*jñāna*).
Next, regarding those who fall into the marks of the two extremes, all are termed deluded consciousness; transcending them constitutes correct wisdom.
Furthermore, that which has the characteristic of being nurtured is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which does not have the characteristic of being nurtured is wisdom (*jñāna*).
Seeing the increase of the three types of supernormal knowledge is called consciousness; being free from such characteristics is wisdom.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of knowledge: namely, knowing arising and ceasing; knowing specific and general characteristics;

and knowing non-arising and non-ceasing. The four vidyās differ according to the objects they respond to: that is, because they respond to ordinary beings, they involve knowing arising and ceasing; because they transform those of the two vehicles...

One knows both the specific and general characteristics because one is the same as a bodhisattva; one knows them as neither arising nor ceasing. Nevertheless, wisdom is solely one, yet it appears diverse according to objects.
Furthermore, the characteristic of non-obstruction is wisdom, while the various obstructed characteristics of the objective realm are consciousness.
When the five consciousnesses are unimpeded in their minds, this is termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*); when they are obstructed by objects, this is "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
The two characters "object-sphere" (*viṣaya*) apply throughout both [the preceding and following sections].

Furthermore, the characteristic of the means for the arising [of consciousness] through the conjunction of the three factors is *vijñāna*. The characteristic of the self-nature of the means when no [external] object exists is *jñāna*.

The six clarities explain that the conjunction of the three factors—the sense organ (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—serves as the means for the arising of consciousness, and this is termed *vijñāna*.
The absence of the three types of expedient means is what is called wisdom.
Furthermore, to apprehend characteristics is consciousness; not to apprehend characteristics is wisdom.
It is clarified that as long as the mind has anything to apprehend, it is termed consciousness; if there is nothing to be apprehended, it is termed wisdom.
One spontaneously attains the realm of noble wisdom because it neither emerges nor enters, like the moon in water.
This refers to the essence of clear wisdom, which is the wisdom spontaneously attained; it has existed from the beginning, and its nature is neither arising nor ceasing.

It is only through the departure from delusion that it is said to arise, and through the obscuration by delusion that it is said to cease. It is like the moon appearing when the water is clear and its reflection sinking when the water is turbid, yet the moon [remains as it is].
The nature is eternally thus; fundamentally, it neither enters nor exits.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The accumulation of karma constitutes consciousness; Non-accumulation constitutes wisdom. One observes all phenomena."
There are seven verses below that explain the thorough penetration of non-existence. Now, both the marks and the wisdom are presented together, while also clarifying the benefits of contemplation:
"Attaining the power of mastery—this is precisely what is called wisdom."
It is said that because the mind is without obstruction, it gives rise [to activity] within the three realms, performs great benefit, and attains mastery of power;
therefore, it is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Binding to objects is the mind (*citta*); the arising of awakened conceptualization is knowledge (*jñāna*).
This indicates the true and the delusive. That which is bound to external objects is the deluded mind; if awakened thought does not arise, it is called true wisdom.
Non-existence and supreme insight are born from this.
This clarifies the benefit of contemplation. That is to say, the eighth stage, the Buddha-ground, possesses supreme wisdom that is effortless; both arise from the awakening of conceptualization.
"Mind, mentation, and consciousness—far removed from the conceptualization of thought.
This clarifies that from the eighth stage upward, there is the supreme wisdom of non-arising, which is free from the ideations of the eight consciousnesses. This is precisely the ultimate reality.
Birth. Attaining the state of non-conceptual dharmas—this is the Son of the Buddha, and not a śrāvaka;
furthermore, it is clearly manifest as superior. If one attains that which is without vitarka, without vicāra, without thought, and without perception, such a one is a bodhisattva.
This does not refer to the two vehicles.
Regarding the patience of tranquil and supreme progress, it is the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata.

Now, as for the term "patience" (*kṣānti*), it encompasses the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sanctity; when categorized generally, there are five types, namely: patience through faith, subduing patience, conforming patience, and the patience of non-arising.
Patience and the other [perfections] are all practices of the bodhisattva. However, the patience of tranquil and supreme progress is the purity of the Buddha’s wisdom.
It gives rise to the excellent ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). All objects of practice are completely transcended;

this is the clear, pure wisdom of the Buddha’s patience, which arises from the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Because it is free from all mental constructions and objects of thought, it is entirely devoid of them. Thus.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-gāthā* states: "The sphere of practice of internal realization, which is signless, Is ineffable and transcends all expression;
It is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) that stills all disputes, Surpassing all discursive thought and conceptualization."
I possess three kinds of wisdom, which the Sage has revealed as the reality. Within those conceptualizations and reflections, all natures are fully encompassed by the luminous Tathāgata.
For the sake of revealing the distinction between the ordinary and the holy, and causing them to awaken to reality, he shows that there are three wisdoms; yet in truth, they are one.
The Way: whatever is contemplated by that Perfect Awakening, there is no object not encompassed. This is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of tranquility;
it is not shared with the two vehicles. This wisdom is free from all that exists.
This clarifies that those of the two vehicles do not correspond with the Buddha’s wisdom.
By means of this wondrous wisdom, one is detached from all that exists and abandons attachment to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because the perspective of the śrāvakas arises from such attachment as their mental state, for this reason they do not accord with the Buddha’s wisdom.
Transcending all mental objects, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is pure;
transcending all minds, this is the Buddha-wisdom. Having attained supreme wisdom, it is free from all that exists.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are nine types of theories of transformation among the non-Buddhists, from which the views of transformation arise.

Herein, I clarify transformation in order to manifest the meaning of the preceding consciousnesses. "Transformation" is a general designation for the causal conditions of both the subjective mind and the objective world.
"Either the object changes and the mind transforms, or the mind changes and the object transforms. This is the initial general statement.
That which is called "the transformation of form and location":
"form" refers to the primary retribution (the body), while "location" refers to the secondary retribution (the environment).
Transformation of characteristics refers to differences such as blue and yellow, as well as distinctions between male and female.
Transformation of causes—
One calculates that all phenomena arise from causes and undergo transformation;
yet one calculates that what belongs to "me" is fixed and indestructible.
The view of transformation consists of four propositions; it is the knowledge of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) regarding the transformation of intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
One grasps at the true and the false, the good and the evil, as well as the four great elements, each as having its own substantial nature.
Because conditions clearly undergo transformation, one calculates that these conditions can manifest the fruit; therefore, it is called "clearly manifest."
The transformations produced are distinct and clear;
one clings to the effect as arising from conditions. The characteristics of phenomena are not erroneous, yet the phenomena themselves undergo transformation.
"Mahāmati, when one calculates all conditioned phenomena,
this is called the ninefold view of transformation. It is because of this that all non-Buddhists give rise to theories of existence and non-existence, and theories of birth and transformation."

Previously, the treatise was introduced by transcending views; now, it is concluded by relying on views to give rise to the treatise. Thus, views and the basis for the treatise depend upon one another, and both are termed "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
What is transformation of shape and location?
From here below, the explanation is clarified. First, the subsequent is illustrated by means of the initial. Now, the first transformation is cited for examination:
namely, the perception of differences in shape and location (*saṃsthāna-deśa*).
This refers to the reckoning that there are distinct variations in shape and location; this clarifies the explanation in terms of phenomena (*dharma-nirdeśa*).
For example, when gold is transformed into various vessels, diverse shapes and forms appear, yet the nature of the gold does not change.

Next, an external analogy is raised: the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain that derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) undergoes transformation, but they do not say this refers to the transformation of its fundamental nature (*dhātu*).
It is like gold fashioned into vessels or clothing; only the derived objects undergo change, while the nature of the gold remains unaltered.
The transformation of all natures is likewise so.
It is also like this regarding the transformation of all forms, locations, and so forth. This concludes the initial explanation.
There are some non-Buddhists who harbor such false imaginings, even extending to the false imagination of the transformation of phenomena.
Now, citing the first [point] to encompass all eight, this serves as a general introduction to the enumeration of their calculations.
That [reality] is neither identical nor different;
from here below follows the explanation and refutation. This is the initial thesis. For the Sage is not identical [to that], and his vision is likewise not different [from it].
Because delusion is itself truth and phenomena are themselves principle, they accord with one another yet are not identical.
This is because of delusive thought;
however, because ordinary beings are deluded, they differ from the sages.

One should understand that all such transformations of nature are exemplified by these nine aforementioned types, which serve as analogies for various views. Thus, one should know that while the paths of ordinary beings and sages differ, the ways of the true and the delusive diverge.
This sentence applies universally to both the preceding and following sections.
For example, when milk, curd, wine, fruit, and so forth undergo transformation, non-Buddhists (tīrthika) falsely imagine this as a process of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).

This passage cites the characteristics of such worldly false views regarding transformation—such as the transformation of milk into curd—to serve as an analogy for the previously mentioned [erroneous] views.
Raw wine becomes cooked; raw fruit is likewise. There are many such instances. In these cases, there is no transformation;
whether existent or non-existent, it is a manifestation of one's own mind. External natures have neither existence nor non-existence.
This refutes the characteristics of the deluded views of ordinary beings.
Mahāmati, it is thus that ignorant and foolish sentient beings cultivate their own false conceptualizations.

To clarify those ordinary and foolish beings, [it is shown] that because of the habitual perfuming of delusion, they produce such views. This is a general summary of the delusions of ordinary and foolish beings.
"O Mahāmati, there is no dharma that arises or ceases, just as one perceives the arising of forms in a magical illusion or a dream.

This explains the aforementioned [teaching] that [dharmas] are neither identical nor different; it means that the noble ones realize the nature of all dharmas to be neither arising nor ceasing, just as one perceives a magical illusion."
Form is fundamentally without transformation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Shape, location, and time undergo transformation; The four great elements and the sense faculties, And the intermediate state (antarābhava) arise in succession."
The verses on the delusive nature of false conceptualization consist of two parts. These refute the views of non-Buddhists and those of the Hīnayāna, namely:

the externalist calculation that form, location, time, and the sense faculties all undergo transformation; and the further calculation that after discarding a previous body in various realms of existence, one continues via the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
That which is "arisen" is what is seen by those of the Two Vehicles;

it is most excellent regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), yet it is not like their false conceptualizations (*parikalpa*). Nevertheless, worldly dependent origination is like a city of the *gandharvas*.
This verse describes the noble vision (*ārya-darśana*). That is to say, regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the Buddha differs from the deluded perceptions of ordinary beings;

he understands that phenomena arising from conditions are like a city of *gandharvas* (an illusory city). Now, this noble vision is presented in order to cause others to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the meaning of the continuity of all dharmas and the meaning of liberation.
I now request this by raising the topics of bondage and liberation; however, within these, the phenomena of birth-and-death, nirvana, and so forth are fully contained."
I wish to cause sentient beings to transcend the two views and enter the Middle Way, thereby providing a distant answer to the previous question: "Who binds and who is liberated?
This is achieved by skillfully discerning the characteristics of all phenomena as being either continuous or non-continuous.
To clarify the benefits that follow: this is a restatement of the preceding thesis.

I and the various bodhisattvas are well-versed in all skillful means regarding the continuity [of existence]; we do not fall into the continuity of attachment to the literal meaning as it has been explained.

First, the provisional benefit of universal access is clarified. This means that understanding the Buddha’s skillful means in teaching regarding continuity is intended to cause one to leave continuity behind;
thus, one is internally unbound and does not cling to verbal designations. The teaching on non-continuity is likewise so.
What is presented here is but one side; by analogy, the rest may be understood.
He is skilled in the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas, as well as in the awakening that is free from the conceptualization of words, letters, and speech.
Next, the benefit of relinquishing the expressive means is clarified: having understood bondage and liberation, one does not become obstructed by words, phrases, or conceptual awakening.
He travels through all buddha-fields, possessing the seal of the power of mastery over infinite assemblies, supernatural penetrations, and dhāraṇīs,
manifesting various transformations and illuminating them with radiant light.

The third is the arising of transformative benefit. That is to say, if one hears this teaching, one will be able to travel through Buddha-fields, manifesting oneself surrounded by a multitude, possessing the mastery of the ten powers, and attaining the two types of retention (dhāraṇī) regarding words and meanings, as well as the seal of the three emptinesses.
One will manifest various transformations and emit great radiance.
Awakened wisdom skillfully enters the ten inexhaustible phrases. There is no practice involving expedient means;

the four clarities are of effortless benefit. This refers to attaining the Buddha-wisdom and wondrously awakening to the ten vows; without relying on expedient means, one transforms beings spontaneously.
This clarifies the teaching of the Dharma.
It is like the sun, the moon, the maṇi jewel, and the four great elements.

Next, seven similes are presented to demonstrate that [the Buddha] is without deliberate effort. Just as the sun and moon shine without thought, and likewise the wish-fulfilling gem grants desires without intention;
furthermore, as the earth supports, water moistens, fire ripens, and wind sustains—these accomplish their functions without conscious reflection. So it is with the Buddha.
The Sattvavastu is also like this:
in all stages, one is free from the marks and views of one's own false imaginings; seeing all phenomena as being like illusions, dreams, and so forth, one enters the body of the Buddha-stage.

The five sciences yield the benefit of attaining the fruit: that is, being free from delusion throughout the stages (*bhūmi*), comprehending all phenomena as being like illusions, dreams, and so forth, and awakening to those stages to realize the *dharmakāya*.
Within the realm of all sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each and guides them.

The preceding [section] concerned self-benefit; now, self-benefit for others is presented: that is, preaching the Dharma and providing instruction to sentient beings according to what is appropriate for each.

They cause all beings to abide securely in the realization that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, and so forth; they lead them to transcend the categories of existence and non-existence, as well as the conceptual constructions of arising and ceasing and the meanings of divergent verbal expressions. Their bodies become increasingly sublime.

Furthermore, they cause them to abide in the realization that all things are like illusions and dreams, and to be free from the deluded conceptions of existence and non-existence, arising and ceasing;
moreover, they cause them not to cling to words and their meanings, so that they may realize the Dharmakāya and become increasingly sublime.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake.
This clarifies the Buddha’s response, first praising, exhorting, and granting permission to speak.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your teaching.
Mahāmati paid his respects with disciplined reverence.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: “Regarding all immeasurable dharmas, there is a continuous attachment to the characteristics of their meanings as they have been described.”

From here below, there is a detailed response. It clarifies that all sentient beings, regarding all phenomena, give rise to views of continuity based on their conceptualizations following verbal designations;
this constitutes the general heading.
Specifically, it refers to the continuity of attachment to signs.
Next, the enumeration is clarified. This refers to seeing and hearing regarding phenomena (*nimitta*), whereby a continuity arises;
it is the conceptual attachment to this continuity, which means being attached to the mental engagement with conditions.
The continuity of clinging to existence and non-existence;
upon hearing of existence and non-existence, one gives rise to clinging;
and the continuity of clinging to the false imaginings of birth and non-birth.
Hearing that there is arising according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and non-arising according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one gives rise to a view of continuity.
One then clings to the continuity of the conceptual construction of extinction and non-extinction.
Furthermore, hearing that the unwholesome has extinction while wholesome dharmas do not have extinction, one follows these words and calculates accordingly, giving rise to a view of continuity.
The continuity of conceptual attachment to the vehicles and non-vehicles;
furthermore, upon hearing of the vehicles and non-vehicles, one gives rise to conceptual attachment;
and the continuity of conceptual attachment to the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Furthermore, having heard that the realm of ordinary beings is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) while the realm of the noble ones is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one gives rise to conceptual attachment.
Thus, there is a continuous succession of false conceptualizations regarding the specific characteristics of each stage (*bhūmi*).
Moreover, having heard that the various stages possess substantial essence and characteristics, one becomes attached to them.
From the continuity of attachment to the conceptualization of what has never been heard,
and because of the attachment to views arising from long-standing false habitual tendencies,
there are non-Buddhist outsiders who rely on the continuity of attachment to conceptualization regarding the categories of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, views such as those concerning existence and non-existence serve as the basis for outsiders to give rise to a continuous stream of conceptualization.
Likewise, through the lack of hearing [the true teaching], there arises a continuous stream of deluded attachment to the three vehicles or the one vehicle.
Moreover, upon hearing the teaching of the three vehicles or the one vehicle, one gives rise to a view that speculates on their reality.
"Mahāmati, this and other ordinary, ignorant beings continue in the succession of their own false imaginings.

This concludes the three points of summary. "This" refers to what was listed in the preceding text; "others" refers to those mentioned generally. Both are merely the false visions of the own-minds of ordinary, ignorant beings.
Because of this continuity, the deluded thoughts of ordinary fools arise;
through this continuity, foolish delusions are produced. This is a general explanation of the principle, like a silkworm making its cocoon.
Next, the illustration is explained:
by the threads of deluded thought, one entangles oneself and entangles others, clinging to the characteristics of existence and non-existence as they continue in succession.

Now, the teaching of the Dharma is clarified: it refers to the ordinary, ignorant beings of the three realms who further entangle and bind one another with the threads of the two views, which are even more severe [than those of deluded thought].

"O Mahāmati, as for that silkworm, within it there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity. The original [text] states: [The opponent says: "World-Honored One, if all dharmas are without self-nature, then how can there be the arising and ceasing of the world? Furthermore, World-Honored One, if all dharmas are without self-nature, then what is the cause and condition for the arising of the world? And what is the cause and condition for its ceasing? How can there be the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, or the attainment of the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha? How can there be the stage of a Bodhisattva, or the attainment of the fruit of a Buddha? World-Honored One, if all dharmas are without self-nature, then how can there be the distinctions of the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four nutriments, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four truths, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, the eight liberations, the nine successive stages of meditative dwelling, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so forth? Furthermore, World-Honored One, if all dharmas are without self-nature, then how can there be the distinction between the three vehicles, or the attainment of the fruit of a Stream-enterer, a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat? How can there be the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, or the attainment of the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha? How can there be the stage of a Bodhisattva, or the attainment of the fruit of a Buddha? World-Honored One, if all dharmas are without self-nature, then how can there be the distinctions of the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four nutriments, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four truths, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, the eight liberations, the nine successive stages of meditative dwelling, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so forth? The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, you should know that all dharmas are indeed without self-nature. Why is this? Because they are devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing. Mahāmati, if all dharmas possessed the characteristic of arising, they would not be devoid of self-nature. If they possessed the characteristic of ceasing, they would likewise not be devoid of self-nature. However, Mahāmati, because all dharmas are devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing, they are therefore devoid of self-nature. Furthermore, Mahāmati, if all dharmas were not devoid of self-nature, then there would be no liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Because all dharmas are devoid of self-nature, one attains liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Furthermore, Mahāmati, if all dharmas were not devoid of self-nature, then there would be no distinction between the three vehicles, nor would there be the attainment of the fruits of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, Non-returner, or Arhat; nor would there be the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, nor the attainment of the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha; nor would there be the stage of a Bodhisattva, nor the attainment of the fruit of a Buddha. Because all dharmas are devoid of self-nature, there is the distinction between the three vehicles, and there is the attainment of the fruits of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, Non-returner, and Arhat; there is the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, and the attainment of the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha; there is the stage of a Bodhisattva, and the attainment of the fruit of a Buddha.
