There is neither bondage nor liberation. Second, regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there are likewise no two characteristics that can be maintained. Both the meaning and the force [of the teaching] are fully encompassed;
the summary is complete.
This is because one perceives all phenomena as quiescent, and thus deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise.
This is the explanation. Because one perceives that quiescence is devoid of delusion, neither bondage nor liberation exists.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives all phenomena as quiescent.
This refers to those who have realized tranquility, namely the bodhisattvas; the meaning of this phrase encompasses both the preceding and the following sections.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, they awaken to the fact that external natures—whether existent or non-existent—are merely manifestations of their own minds and are ultimately non-existent.
This clarifies the aforementioned Bodhisattvas. Because they realize that external objects lack intrinsic nature, they perceive that what appears to the mind is fundamentally non-existent.
They accordingly observe that all things, whether existent or non-existent, are manifestations of their own mind and are devoid of characteristics.

Now, regarding the source of this nature of clear comprehension: because this bodhisattva accords with and enters into realization, the fundamental mind manifests before him, whereby he immediately knows that all natures, including the two extremes of existence and non-existence, are entirely without marks.
"Because one sees that the continuity [of the mind] is quiescent.
Regarding "the external lacks intrinsic nature": because one sees that the entire continuity is completely quiescent, this phrase applies throughout both the preceding and following sections.
Regarding all phenomena, there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity;
this is the concluding summary.
Mahāmati, therein there is neither bondage nor liberation. Others, falling into error through not awakening to reality as it is, perceive continuity and liberation.

This second pair designates the two views of ordinary beings and noble ones. Because those noble ones have realized reality as it is (*yathābhūta*), they are fundamentally neither bound nor liberated.
All other ordinary beings, however, fall into non-reality and perceive the existence of bondage and liberation.
Why is this so? This phrase under investigation refers to a meaning that applies to both ordinary beings and sages;
it means that among all phenomena, there is neither existence nor non-existence, because no sentient being can be apprehended.
This pair explains the two views. To explain the noble view (*ārya-dṛṣṭi*), it is said that regarding all phenomena, both existence and non-existence are entirely non-existent;

furthermore, no sentient being can be apprehended. By means of this single word, the upper and lower [extremes] are encompassed, clarifying that both person and phenomena are neither [existent nor non-existent].
This clarifies the noble view. Furthermore, to explain the ordinary view (*pṛthagjana-dṛṣṭi*), it is said that regarding...

Regarding the existence and non-existence of all phenomena: this existence and non-existence is what sentient beings perceive. These two characters, "existence" and "non-existence," encompass both the preceding and the following [sections].
This explains how ordinary beings fall into non-reality. That two distinct explanations employ the same phrasing is likewise a marvel of the Sanskrit language.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three types of continuity for fools.
The third [category] clarifies that continuity is actually non-continuity with respect to the three poisons; this first [category] indicates the number by reference to persons.
This refers to greed, hatred, delusion, and craving. Regarding the future existence accompanied by joy and craving, the subsequent explanation states:
because of the three poisons and craving, the fool will inevitably obtain retribution in the future;
that retribution is likewise accompanied by joy and craving, arising simultaneously with the body.
Because of this continuity, there is the continuity of the realms of existence (*gati*).
Because the three poisons are not severed, one undergoes successive births within the five aggregates and the five realms of existence.
That which is "continuous" refers to the continuity of the five realms.
This is a further explanation. Because those three poisons continue in succession, they lead to rebirth in the five destinies. The above is a general summary of the views.
Mahāmati, for one whose succession has been severed, there is neither the characteristic of succession nor the characteristic of non-succession.
Next is the refutation. This means that by realizing reality as it is, the continuity of the three poisons perishes; thus, both bondage and liberation are equally purified.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, through the conditions of the triple combination, one forms attachments based on skillful means; thus, the consciousnesses arise in uninterrupted succession.

Fourth, by means of the three conditions, the three liberations are clarified. That is to say, through the expedient means of the three conditions—root, object, and consciousness—the karmic consciousness continues to arise.
Through expedient attachment, there is then continuity.
Next, the manifestation of results is explained. This means that because of attachment to the expedient means of the three conditions, there is the continuation and rebirth of existence (*bhava*).
The above is a general summary of the calculations.
When the consciousness conditioned by the harmony of the three is severed, one perceives the three liberations; then, all continuities cease to arise.

This, too, is refuted. It is said that when one realizes objects have no marks, the nature of the faculties is inherently empty, and consciousness has nothing to aspire toward—this is precisely the three liberations.
From what, then, could continuity arise?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Unreal conceptualization—this is called the characteristic of continuity.
This clarifies that because it is not real, it is falsely called 'continuity.'"
If one knows that reality, the net of continuity is severed;
if one knows reality, continuity does not arise.
Through ignorance regarding all natures, one is grasped by verbal designations.
If one lacks knowledge of the Dharma and grasps it merely according to the words,
they are like that silkworm which weaves its own web and becomes entangled within it.
(This verse illustrates the preceding metaphor.)
"Fools are bound by conceptual construction; they do not observe the continuity [of this process].
Because they do not observe it, they mistake what is delusory for a binding.
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the Blessed One has said, 'By means of various conceptual constructions, one conceptually constructs those various [objects]...'"
Nature.
From here below, the distinctions are severed. Since the Buddha previously stated that both bondage and liberation are false, a challenge is now about to be raised; therefore, this is restated.
That is to say, the eleven kinds of bondage and liberation mentioned above are mutually related to one another, hence the term "this and that" (*teṣu teṣu*); because they are not real...
Therefore, it is called "false imagination" (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, this false imagination consists in reckoning that there is such a nature as bondage and liberation;
yet, those do not possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for they are merely the nature of false imagination itself.

Furthermore, as the World-Honored One has taught: there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to that which is bound or liberated; it is merely a false attachment to the existence of an intrinsic nature.
The above constitutes Mahāmati’s restatement of what the Buddha has taught.

Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "If it is only the nature of false conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and not the nature of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), then they cannot be mutually dependent.

Next, to clarify the established tenet: if one says that bondage and liberation are merely false conceptualization and do not possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) such that they could be mutually dependent."
Is it not the case that the World-Honored One has thus stated that afflictions and purification are without intrinsic nature?
This is the third formal objection. Is it not so that the Buddha taught that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are devoid of essence, thereby falling into the error of viewing things as empty?
Because all phenomena (dharmas) are of the nature of false conceptualization and lack intrinsic nature.

Fourth, this explains the intent behind the objection: since the Buddha previously stated that the natures of bondage, liberation, and so forth—namely, all phenomena—exist only through false conceptualization and fundamentally lack intrinsic nature.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "So it is, so it is;
it is just as you have said. Now, to clarify the Buddha’s response: he simply confirms the preceding objection as a seal of approval, thereby constituting the answer.

That is to say, I truly declare that the natures of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, bondage and liberation, and so forth, are all empty. Emptiness is itself the principle (*tattva*); yet this principle is not non-existent.
What is there to be abandoned?
Mahāmati, it is not like the reality of the imagined nature of self-nature held by foolish people;
this establishes the aforementioned meaning of emptiness, meaning that because those foolish people do not grasp at [reality] as real through their deluded attachments, existence is negated.
Regarding the statement on emptiness: if the mind is free from obstructions and attachments, there is nothing that can be emptied.
This is the self-nature of deluded conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);

it does not possess the characteristics of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). Now, to further refute emotional views: this so-called bondage and liberation arises merely from the deluded conceptualization of ordinary beings; in reality, it is not so.

It is not existent. However, Mahāmati, just as there is the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom— known by the noble ones, seen by the noble ones, and perceived by the noble eye of wisdom— in this same way,
one knows that intrinsic nature.

The former [teachings] sent forth the statement that "existence is empty. Now, the fragments of the Truth are explained. Since one is already free from emotional attachments, the Truth shines forth with spontaneous clarity;
it is not the same as the delusions of ordinary beings. Therefore, it is said that noble wisdom possesses an intrinsic nature and is known by the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).

Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "If it is as you have taught, that the noble ones know by means of the noble knowledge, see by means of the noble vision, and through the eye of wisdom—and not by the divine eye nor the fleshly eye—they know the nature of self-nature in this way."

Because the Buddha’s supreme illumination has already sent forth words declaring that [the self] is real, I fear that upon hearing this teaching, one might immediately give rise to the view of existence (*bhavadrṣṭi*).
For this reason, Mahāmati, apprehending the doubts of sentient beings and wishing to entrust himself to the Buddha to raise an objection, he makes this citation.
It is not like the deluded conceptualizations of foolish people;

for the Buddha has taught that true reality is the noble knowledge (*āryajñāna*) which appears as if it exists within objects. Therefore, Mahāmati below raises five difficulties, all of which arise based on what preceded.
Now, this is the first among the difficulties concerning the distinctness of ordinary beings and noble ones; this is the definitive statement, namely:
If this is indeed the noble knowledge, and not that which is known and seen by fools through the divine eye or the fleshly eye,
World-Honored One, how do fools depart from such false conceptualization?

Next, the formal presentation of the objection is clarified: If, as stated above, the ultimate truth is known only by the noble ones, how can ordinary, deluded beings rely upon that truth to abandon the false?
Because they do not perceive the matter of the noble nature (*ārya-dharma*), this is the third objection; it is also called an explanation.
Since the matter of the noble nature is not perceived by the ignorant, O Bhagavān, that [ignorance] is neither inverted nor non-inverted.

Second, clarifying the difficulty that the realm of ordinary beings is not inverted: If the Real were not the realm of ordinary beings, then those ordinary beings would neither possess the two views of being inverted nor being non-inverted.
Since ordinary beings do not enter the state of the Sage, they do not overturn the Real; therefore, this is a "double negation. Furthermore, this is clearly stated in the introductory exposition.
Why is this so? Next, what is meant by saying that ordinary persons are neither inverted nor non-inverted?
It means that they do not realize the nature and self-nature of the reality of the noble ones.
Third, the explanation of the reason: namely, because the realm of the sages is not what ordinary beings can perceive, nor does it involve overturning the true to give rise to the false.
This explains that such ordinary beings are not themselves subject to perversion.
This is because one does not perceive [them] apart from the characteristics of existence and non-existence.

Second, it clarifies that noble wisdom is free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence; since this is not something known or seen by ordinary beings, it establishes the aforementioned point that it is not a perverted view.
World-Honored One, the noble ones do not perceive things in this way as they are falsely conceptualized, because they do not take the realm of self-characteristics as their objective domain.

Third, in the section clarifying the difficulty regarding how the noble ones are equally subject to the inversions of ordinary beings, this first part presents both [the thesis and the reason] together; it is also a concessive argument, meaning that the noble ones—
Since there is such a true nature, how is it not like the way ordinary people conceive of things, grasping at objects and persisting in their existence within material entities?
World-Honored One, that too is the characteristic of self-nature; the self-nature of conceptual construction manifests in this way, yet you do not speak of its cause.

Next is the formal restatement [of the objection]. This means that if the Sage were to appear by means of false attachments as an ordinary person does, and furthermore did not explain the reason why he is real,
it would be because there is no cause [for such an appearance].

The third line presents a general objection: it clarifies that the true realm of the Sage would fall into the error of causelessness, because it would entail falling into the views of essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

The fourth part explains the reason for this charge of causelessness: it refers to the non-Buddhist (Tīrthika) calculation that essences such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) do not arise from causes. The world...
Venerable One, if that were so, you would fall into this view:
that objects are distinct and not as they appear, which leads to the fault of infinite regress. Fifth, the correct explanation:

the noble ones are identical to ordinary beings in their inversion; that is, while ordinary beings deviate from the Noble Path, the fault [of such deviation] would otherwise be infinite. If the noble ones were different...
It should also be thus for ordinary beings, O Bhagavān, because they do not perceive the intrinsic nature and characteristics of reality.
This is the sixth summary: since the Buddha has taught that the noble realm is not perceived by ordinary beings.

The World-Honored One is likewise not the cause for the nature of imagined self-nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Regarding the characteristics of that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), how could he be deluded?

This is the fourth point: the objection that the realm of ordinary beings is not deluded. Since the realm of the sages is not that of ordinary beings, if it does not arise from the sages, how can it be so designated?
Are those ordinary beings alone considered deluded? This is the initial thesis.
It is not false imagination; one knows false imagination as it truly is.
Next, the text explains that while ordinary beings do not realize it is false, the noble ones awaken to it and know it as it truly is, whereas we ordinary beings take it to be false.
World-Honored One, false imagination is distinct, and the characteristics of intrinsic nature are distinct.
These two points are presented together to mean that the false is distinct from the true, and the true is distinct from the false;
this clarifies the difference between the ultimate and the conventional, demonstrating that ordinary beings are not [merely] false.
"World-Honored One, the characteristics of the imagined nature have dissimilar causes.
Next, you set forth two distinct causes and further clarify that the realm of ordinary beings is not unreal; that is to say, ordinary beings take false imagination as their cause."
The Noble Ones take the characteristic of true intrinsic nature as their cause. Since these two causes are distinct, the ordinary person is not deluded [in that regard].
How could they each not be free from false conceptualization? The foolish do not perceive things as they truly are.
The fourth point is a reprimand and interrogation: "If the two truths are indeed distinct, why is it that the sages are each non-delusory while the ignorant are not in accordance with reality?
This reproach is misplaced and inconsistent.
Nevertheless, for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon deluded thoughts, it is taught that they exist according to the characteristics of deluded thought and do not truly exist as such;
this is the fifth [point], the "knot. Because the sages desire to cause ordinary people to leave behind delusion, they consequently speak of the delusions of ordinary people.
It is not that these exist as real entities; yet, I, an ordinary person, am truly not deluded.
World-Honored One, for what reason do you negate the existence of the view of "existence" and "non-existence" in sentient beings, and [negate] attachment to the intrinsic nature of phenomena?

This is the fifth [point]: the noble ones falling into the fallacy of existence and non-existence. This is the initial heading that rebukes the noble ones and excludes the ordinary persons. That is to say:
for what reason does the Buddha exclude those ordinary persons from giving rise to the two views of existence and non-existence?

To be attached to the sphere of activity of noble wisdom is to fall into the view of existence (*bhavadrṣṭi*). To preach that the dharmas of emptiness lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) follows this;

it clarifies that the noble ones are equal to ordinary people. This refers to the preceding passage which states that if there were noble wisdom to be conceptualized, that would itself constitute falling into existence.
Furthermore, it is taught that bondage and liberation are without intrinsic nature; this too falls into emptiness.
Yet, the self-nature of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) is explained as a real entity—this clarifies the point of connection.
Moreover, the Buddha himself has spoken in two different ways, both stating that it is my noble wisdom that brings benefit.
This is the Dharma-gate. Although the five difficulties have been clarified above, the general meaning resides solely within the two extremes of emptiness and existence.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not that I teach a dharma of emptiness that is non-existent; nor do I fall into the view of existence."
The second section clarifies the Tathāgata’s extensive response. It demonstrates that what the Buddha has taught does not fall into the two extremes of emptiness or existence;
this generally refutes the previous objections.
He explains the nature of the reality of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna-svabhāva*), yet he does so for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon phrases that provoke fear.
From here on, the text provides an exegesis of the assembly. It clarifies that although the Buddha spoke of existence, this does not contradict emptiness;

yet, because people are terrified of emptiness and utterly unable to initiate cultivation, he speaks of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). This is discussed in terms of principle (*tattva*); how could it possibly abide in existence?

Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been attached to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things, as well as to the characteristics of attachment to the intrinsic nature of the objects of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

When they see and hear the teaching on emptiness, it is subsequently explained that this teaching of emptiness does not contradict existence, because sentient beings have long been habituated to its power; thus, upon hearing the discourse on bondage and liberation, [they do not immediately realize the ultimate truth].

Failing to understand the skillful means of noble wisdom, they give rise to conceptual attachment; therefore, emptiness is taught. This is intended to dispel [the notion of] existence—what "emptiness" could there be [apart from that]?
Mahāmati, I do not speak of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

This clarifies the summary that the Buddha does not speak of a self-nature of emptiness or existence. However, the preceding section has generally explained the skillful means for harmonizing these views.
Mahāmati, I abide in the dharma of emptiness as it is personally realized, which is free from doubt, confusion, and the characteristics of dualistic views.
This is an explanation based on the ultimate reality, clarifying the realization of emptiness as it truly is, which is free from the delusive appearances and views of existence and non-existence.
Now, in citing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the intention is to cause all sentient beings to tread upon the tracks of the Tathāgata.
Having abandoned the views of existence and non-existence regarding the nature of what is manifested by one's own mind,
and having transcended both existence and non-existence, one realizes the previously abandoned marks of delusive perception. Thus,
one becomes sealed with the seal of reality that characterizes the three gates of liberation.
This refers to that which the Buddha has attained: reality free from delusion, the secret seal of the one mind and three emptinesses.
By grasping, transforming, and maintaining faith, one is without obstruction.
Regarding the self-nature of phenomena, one attains abiding through the observation of self-awareness based on conditions;

because one has obtained the seal of reality, one is free from the views and signs of existence and non-existence regarding entities. Regarding the self-nature of the dharma-realm, one abides by observing the internal mind based on conditions;
thus, all views of existence and non-existence regarding entities are entirely abandoned.
It is perfected. Furthermore, it awakens sentient beings; this refers to the meaning of "Buddha" mentioned previously. This is a mutual clarification between the Sanskrit and Chinese terms.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain to you according to your questions."
The Buddha, about to expound [the teaching], first granted his permission.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, do you act? Or do you not act?"

From this point on, Mahāmati requests further instruction; this is the first inquiry. It refers to restating the meaning of "Buddha" as one of the three titles among the ten epithets of the Dharma-body, namely:
that which "rides upon the One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*) as its path, has arrived at Great Wisdom, and has destroyed the thieves of the fetters to attain Perfect Enlightenment.
Is this [attainment] produced through volitional effort (*abhisamskāra*), or is it non-produced? This is the first paired question.
"Is it for the sake of an object?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding such terms and phrases, [teaches] neither as an object nor as a cause."
From this point downward, the Buddha provides the answer. He categorically rejects the question; since it is not based on actual facts, other instances may be understood by analogy.
Why is this so? This is followed by the clarification of the inquiry.
Because both [positions] share the same fault.

This third point collectively refutes the previous questions, showing that the fault does not apply solely to the causal factor of the thing-in-itself (*vastu*), but intends to clarify that the other phrases also entail this same error.
Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were a thing-in-itself...
In the fourth section, the extensive explanation of the refutation, this first part restates the thesis:
"Whether it is a conditioned phenomenon or impermanent.
Next follows the formal explanation: "If the Buddha were a conditioned phenomenon, he would either be identical to a produced thing or fall into the category of the impermanent. This is...
This is the sequential explanation: because of impermanence, all things should be the Tathāgata;
this is a concessive statement (*utkarṣa*). Since they are equally conditioned products, all worldly effects and phenomena should likewise be the Tathāgata.
Neither I nor any of the Buddhas would desire this;
it is a censure. From myself, Śākyamuni, down to all the Buddhas, none would wish to be a Tathāgata by means of that which is impermanent.
If it is not something produced, next, the reason that "it is not something produced" is refuted. This too is first restated:
because nothing is apprehended, the means [of proof] are empty.
Now, as for the dharma of non-action, there is nothing to be attained therein. If this were so, then the Buddha’s wondrous efficacy would be rendered in vain.
This is the explanation provided next.
The Threefold Knowledge (traividya) cites these two analogies— the rabbit’s horn and the son of a barren woman—
to demonstrate that while names exist, reality does not;
for they possess no intrinsic existence whatsoever.
These are the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Because they are equally non-existent, Mahāmati, if there were neither an object nor a cause, then it would be neither existent nor non-existent.

Above, we explained the refutation of each individually; now, we employ the "double negation. Since it is neither an object nor a cause, how could it be stuck in the realm of existence or non-existence?
If it is neither existent nor non-existent, then it transcends the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).
Since it is neither existent nor non-existent, it surpasses the four propositions.
These four propositions are worldly discourse; that which transcends the four propositions does not fall into the four propositions.
Now, that which falls into the [four] propositions is called the mundane world. If one does not fall into the four propositions, it is called "transcending.
Because one does not fall into the four propositions, it is what the wise accept.
The dharma that transcends linguistic categories is realized by the wise.
The meaning of the phrases of all Tathāgatas is likewise so. The wise should know this:

they clearly understand that the nature of the three bodies of the Buddhas transcends the four logical extremes (*catuskoṭi*). Those possessing wisdom should know it thus. This concludes the explanation above.
The Buddhas’ three bodies are free from the meaning of verbal expression; they exhort [beings] to realize this.
Just as I have taught that all phenomena are without self, you should know that this meaning is the nature of selflessness.

This cites the past to corroborate the present. As the Buddha previously taught that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*), one should know that this is precisely the meaning of the Dharma-body being beyond verbal expression.
This absence of self in all phenomena means that they possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and lack extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*).

From here below, its selflessness is explained in order to reveal the Dharmakāya. As for the term "selflessness," it means that there is only the intrinsic nature of emptiness, and no extrinsic nature of false views regarding existence or non-existence.
It is like oxen and horses;
this is a brief illustration of the metaphor.
Mahāmati, for example, the nature of non-oxen and non-horses—that is, the nature of horses and oxen—is in reality neither existent nor non-existent.
This is a precise analogy. For example, suppose there is a horse that is originally not a cow. When one looks at it from a great distance, one calls it a cow;
yet upon approaching and observing it closely, it is not so. And this appearance of a cow is, in reality, neither existent nor non-existent.
It is not that they lack their own characteristics;
that is to say, it is not that the horse lacks its own substantial entity. The above has been explained by way of analogy.
In this same way, Mahāmati, all phenomena do not lack their own characteristics; they possess their own characteristics.
From here below, the principle of conjunction is applied. That is to say, the nature of all phenomena lies neither in existence nor in non-existence, but in the intermediate state between them.
The single character "non-" (非) doubly penetrates both "self" (自), thereby conjoining with the preceding "ox" (牛) to form "the ox is neither existent nor non-existent."
However, this non-self cannot be known by foolish ordinary people;
it clarifies the state beyond existence and non-existence, and is not something that can be known by the foolish practitioners of the Two Vehicles or by followers of external paths.
Because of their deluded imaginings,
it is clarified that these two individuals have both not yet transcended delusion.
Thus, one should know that all phenomena are empty, unarisen, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
This exhortation to realize that all phenomena are empty, unarisen, and devoid of intrinsic nature corresponds to the preceding horse.
This principle of the emptiness of phenomena transcends existence and non-existence; it is the very nature of the Dharmakāya.
Thus, the Tathāgata and the aggregates (skandhas) are neither different nor non-different.

From here on, the text proceeds through specific refutations of views to further clarify that the nature of the three bodies (trikāya) is neither identical nor different. Now, this is explained by means of the aggregates.
This is the initial thesis.
If [the Tathāgata] were not different from the aggregates (*skandha*), he would be impermanent.

This is the subsequent specific citation and refutation; that is to say, since people see the aggregates as impermanent, if the Tathāgata were identical to the aggregates, he too would likewise be so.
"Impermanent. This is a refutation by concession.
If [the Tathāgata] were different [from the aggregates], then skillful means would be empty;
for when worldly people look outside the various aggregates, they find nothing at all. Now, if you say that the Tathāgata is different from the aggregates, why is this so?
Because there is the functional application of compassion and wisdom that benefits both self and others, it is called "emptiness.
If these two were distinct, there would necessarily be a difference between them;
now, the third [section] cites these two views and refutes them. If one were to claim that the Tathāgata and the aggregates are two separate dharmas, then...
There are cases of both difference and non-difference; for now, we shall examine only one side, as can be seen in the following text.
It is like the similarity between the horns of an ox.
This is the meaning of the present passage.
Observing conditioned phenomena, they are neither causeless nor possess a cause; thus, the views of those who propound arising and ceasing are extinguished.
Having already refuted both existence and non-existence as causes, this dual negation reveals the benefit [of the Middle Way].
"What is meant by 'non-arising'? Is it the absence of intrinsic nature?
This first section generally refutes external views; from here below, it clarifies the true non-arising, which is a verse summarizing the preceding prose.
That is to say: what is this "non-arising"? Is it the absence of intrinsic nature?
In order to examine various conditions, there is a teaching called "Unsurpassed Verse" [stating]:
Because this exists in dependence upon conditions, does this non-arising exist?
This name should not be meaningless; it is taught solely for the sake of analytical discrimination.
This verse above states: "If there were dharmas possessing names, I would only wish for you to explain them.
It is not that they lack intrinsic nature or are unarisen; nor is it a matter of merely gathering all things together."
Characteristics are not real characteristics; they are "I" and "mine" due to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
However, these two marks of self are themselves essentially false. Among the five dharmas, they are subsumed under name (*nāman*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
The two types of cessation through appropriation, and the non-arising of the two forms of selflessness.
By means of the suchness of their wisdom, they encompass these two forms of selflessness.
Therefore, Mahāmati, these five dharmas constitute the noble, self-realized wisdom of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas.
The sequential continuity of all the stages (bhūmi) contains within it all the Buddha-dharmas;

it is not merely the five dharmas that encompass the three [natures] and the Buddha. The noble wisdom cultivated by the three vehicles, the stages and positions of practice across all the grounds, and even the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time are all subsumed therein.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the "five dharmas," this is a general enumeration to clarify the five dharmas again from below:
characteristics, names, conceptualization, suchness, and right knowledge.

In this subsequent listing of names, there is a slight departure from the previous order. Previously, the derivative was raised without yet revealing the fundamental; now, the fundamental is raised to encompass the derivative, thereby demonstrating the efficacy of the five dharmas.
Furthermore, it serves to dismantle the attachments held by worldly sentiments.
Mahāmati, as for "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), they have been explained extensively in three ways; here, first, characteristics are distinguished:
when locations, shapes, colors, forms, and so forth appear, these are called characteristics.
Now, the physical form and its constituent parts are collectively termed "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).

In my leisure time from the myriad affairs of state, I have perused the classical texts; therein, I have found those concerning the preservation of the body, the prolongation of life, the pacification of the people, and the maintenance of one's vocation.

Among the classics and histories, the teachings of the Śākya are supreme. Thus, relying upon the Triple Gem and taking refuge in the One Vehicle, I have respectfully completed the transcription of all these scriptural volumes.

May those who read them with a heart of utmost sincerity, for the sake of the state above and all living beings below, pray for a hundred years of life and ten thousand blessings. And may those who hear them not [suffer] for immeasurable kalpas.
They fall into the evil realms; may they distance themselves from this net and together ascend to the other shore.

The *Keian Shukan* and the *Nibirimari-jo* both bear the imperial calligraphy of Emperor Shōmu;
they are collectively known as "Dai-Shōmu" (Great Shōmu), a name derived from the fact that the characters are larger than usual.

This commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* possesses a stroke power that is vigorous and firm; like soaring phoenixes and leaping dragons, it naturally carries the majesty of celestial beings traversing the void.
This refers to the Great Sage-Warrior. It is truly beyond praise; it has been bound in ten layers of silk and treasured as a precious relic.
